title: Motion in the Schwarzschild geometry
part: IV: Orbits, stars, and black holes
one_line_summary: Shows that free motion outside a spherical mass can be analysed without ever writing the geodesic equation: read two conserved quantities (energy and angular momentum per unit rest mass) off the metric's missing coordinates, combine them with the normalization of the four-velocity, and derive the gravitational redshift, a relativistic effective potential with an extra 1/r^3 term, and the radial plunge from rest at infinity, whose finite proper time but divergent Schwarzschild coordinate time at r = 2M sets up the later black-hole chapters.
role_in_book: Third chapter of Part IV. Chapter 20 built Newtonian orbits around an effective potential and Chapter 21 produced the Schwarzschild line element; this chapter is the bridge that turns that metric into trajectories. It supplies the working toolkit (Killing-vector constants of motion, u.u = -1 or 0, the dx/dt = u^i/u^t trick, static-observer vielbeins) that Chapter 23 uses for bound orbits and perihelion precession, Chapter 24 for photon paths, and Chapter 25 for the horizon. Consistent with the book's spiral design, the Killing-vector rule is used as an unproved recipe here and only justified geometrically in Chapter 33, and the puzzle of the infinite coordinate time to reach r = 2M is flagged and deliberately left for Chapter 25.

assumed_background.topic: The Schwarzschild line element and the meaning of its coordinates t, r, theta, phi
Free fall as geodesic motion and the geodesic equation with connection coefficients
Four-velocity, four-momentum, and energy measured by an observer as minus the dot product of momentum with the observer's velocity
Metric components as dot products of coordinate basis vectors, g_{mu nu} = e_mu . e_nu, and index lowering
Orthonormal frames, vielbein components and freely falling frames
Newtonian orbits reduced to one-dimensional motion in an effective potential
Gravitational frequency shift from the equivalence principle
Geometrized units with G = c = 1 so that M stands for GM/c^2
Conservation of energy and angular momentum in central-force problems
Separable first-order ODEs, substitution and partial-fraction integrals giving logarithms

learning_objectives: Reader can scan a metric for coordinates that appear in none of its components and write down the corresponding Killing vectors in component form.
Reader can form the conserved quantities E-tilde = -xi.u and L-tilde = eta.u for Schwarzschild and interpret them as energy and angular momentum per unit rest mass as judged from far away.

Reader can state the normalization u.u = -1 for massive particles (proper time as parameter) and u.u = 0 for light (affine parameter) and explain why it carries information about the kind of particle.

Reader can derive the gravitational redshift formula omega_inf = omega_R (1 - 2M/R)^{1/2} by writing a static observer's four-velocity as a multiple of the time Killing vector and using conservation of xi.p.
Reader can reduce equatorial geodesic motion to the one-dimensional equation E_eff = (1/2)(dr/dtau)^2 + V_eff(r) and identify the extra -M L^2/r^3 term relative to the Newtonian effective potential.
Reader can sketch the relativistic effective potential, explain the inner maximum and the fall to minus infinity at small r, and restore G and c to show the correction is order 1/c^2.
Reader can solve the radial plunge from rest at infinity: E-tilde = 1, dr/dtau = -(2M/r)^{1/2}, the four-velocity components, and r(tau) proportional to (tau_* - tau)^{2/3}.
Reader can integrate dt/dr for the plunge and show that Schwarzschild coordinate time diverges logarithmically as r -> 2M while proper time stays finite.
Reader can contrast the coordinate speed dr/dt, which goes to zero at r = 2M, with the speed measured by a local static observer, which tends to the speed of light there for any infall energy.
Reader can convert coordinate quantities into what a static observer measures using the vielbein factors (1 - 2M/r)^{+1/2} for time and (1 - 2M/r)^{-1/2} for radial distance.
Reader can apply the same toolkit to exercises such as the gravitational clock effect for airborne clocks and the relative speed of two radially separated observers.

teaching_approach.summary: A deliberately economical chapter whose message is that symmetry plus normalization beats brute force. The authors open by admitting that solving the geodesic equation looks daunting, then promise that conserved quantities, exactly as in Newtonian orbit problems, will do the work. A boxed three-step recipe (look for absent coordinates, name the Killing vector, dot it with the velocity) is given without proof and immediately applied to Schwarzschild. Every later result uses only these ingredients, most of them packaged as shaded Example blocks: the redshift (argued in running text rather than an Example) via a static observer whose velocity is proportional to the time Killing vector, the effective potential via u.u = -1, a Newtonian-limit check by restoring G and c, and the radial plunge with its three clocks and two speeds. The recurring pedagogical contrast is coordinate quantities versus what a local observer actually measures, handled with vielbein factors. Surprising results (frozen coordinate time at 2M) are stated, graphed, and explicitly postponed to Chapter 25.
narrative_arc: Motivating worry: finding orbits seems to require the full geodesic equation and all the Christoffel symbols of the Schwarzschild metric
Reassurance by analogy: Newtonian orbit problems collapse once energy and angular momentum conservation are used, so look for relativistic counterparts
Recipe (stated, not proved): coordinates absent from the metric give Killing vectors, and their dot product with a geodesic's tangent is constant
Application: t and phi are absent, giving xi = e_t and eta = e_phi and the constants E-tilde and L-tilde, interpreted per unit rest mass and as seen from infinity
Second ingredient: u.u = -1 or 0 encodes whether the free-falling object is massive or light
First payoff (photons): static observer's velocity written as (1 - 2M/r)^{-1/2} xi, so conserved xi.p yields the gravitational redshift in one line
Toolbox recap as a margin checklist beside the start of §22.3: normalization, Killing rule, and dx/dt = (dx/dtau)/u^t
Second payoff (massive particles): substitute E-tilde and L-tilde into u.u = -1 for equatorial motion to get an energy equation with a relativistic effective potential
Check: compare with the Newtonian effective potential of Chapter 20; restore G and c to show the new term is a 1/c^2 correction scaling as 1/r^3
Measurement caveat: coordinate components must be converted with the static-observer vielbein, and moving observers need their own frame
Worked application: radial plunge from rest at infinity; derive u^mu, proper-time law r(tau) and coordinate-time law t(r)
Surprise: infinite coordinate time but finite proper time to reach r = 2M; explicitly deferred to Chapter 25
Second surprise: coordinate speed vanishes at 2M while a local static observer measures the infall speed approaching c
Hand-off to Chapter 23 on orbits; exercises extend to proper acceleration, escape speed, Hafele-Keating clocks and relative velocities
signature_moves: Replace the geodesic equation by 'conserved quantities from absent coordinates plus u.u = -1', presented as a boxed, numbered recipe.
Express a static observer's four-velocity as a scalar multiple of the time-translation Killing vector so that measured energies become ratios of normalization factors.
Force the relativistic result into the exact algebraic shape of the Newtonian effective-potential equation of Chapter 20, then point to the single extra term.
Define the Newtonian energy through E-tilde = (mc^2 + E_N)/mc^2 and restore G and c to read the relativistic correction as an order-1/c^2 addition.
Put the same plunging particle on three graphs (r against tau, r against t, speed against r) so the coordinate-versus-proper contrast is visual.
Use margin notes to carry supporting derivations (the observer-at-infinity energy rule, the falling-frame vielbein, the coordinate escape velocity) so the main text stays short.
State an alarming result plainly (the infaller never reaches 2M in coordinate time) and promise its resolution later rather than resolving it immediately.

sections.title: Chapter opening: from metric to motion
sections.summary: Two literary epigraphs about being tossed by the stars and setting off on pilgrimage frame the topic. The Schwarzschild line element and its four non-zero components are recalled, and the programme is announced: study free fall as geodesic motion, find richer behaviour than in Newtonian gravity, and avoid solving the geodesic equation directly by leaning on conserved quantities and the normalization of the four-velocity.
key_moves: Quote the Schwarzschild metric (22.2) and list g_tt, g_rr, g_theta theta, g_phi phi in the margin (22.1).
Observe that the geodesic equation with all connection coefficients looks heavy.
Promise that, as in Newtonian orbit theory, conserved quantities plus u.u = -1 or 0 will suffice.

sections.title: Constants of the motion
sections.summary: Gives an operational rule for conserved quantities: if no metric component depends on a coordinate x^alpha then e_alpha is a Killing vector and its dot product with the tangent of any geodesic is constant. For Schwarzschild this yields the time Killing vector xi = e_t and the rotational one eta = e_phi, and hence E-tilde = (1 - 2M/r) dt/dtau and L-tilde = r^2 sin^2(theta) dphi/dtau, read as energy and angular momentum per unit rest mass. A margin note explains why the energy is the one measured by a static observer far away, whose four-velocity is xi. The section closes by fixing the tangent's norm, -1 for massive particles parametrized by proper time and 0 for light with an affine parameter.
concepts: conservation law from a Killing vector
conserved energy per unit rest mass
conserved angular momentum per unit rest mass
key_moves: Shaded recipe: a coordinate missing from every metric component gives a Killing vector e_alpha, and its dot product with the geodesic tangent is constant (22.3).
Spot that Schwarzschild components depend only on r and theta, so t and phi give xi and eta (22.4, 22.5).
Evaluate xi.u = u_t = g_tt u^t and define E-tilde as its negative (22.6-22.8).
Margin argument: a static observer at infinity has u_obs = xi in flat asymptotic space, so -p.xi is the energy measured there.
Evaluate eta.u = u_phi = r^2 sin^2 theta u^phi (22.9) and note it reduces to r^2 phi-dot in the equatorial plane.
Fix the particle type through u.u = -1 (22.10) or u.u = 0 (22.11).

sections.title: Gravitational redshift
sections.summary: A photon travels radially outwards from a static observer at radius R to one at infinity. Measured energy is minus the dot product of the photon momentum with the observer's velocity. A static observer's velocity has only a time component fixed by normalization, (1 - 2M/r)^{-1/2}, so it equals that factor times the time Killing vector. Because xi.p is constant along the photon's geodesic, the measured frequencies at R and at infinity differ only by the normalization factor, giving omega_inf = omega_R (1 - 2M/R)^{1/2}. Light loses energy climbing out, and the frequency needed at R to deliver a fixed frequency far away grows without bound as R approaches 2M.
key_moves: Note that what is conserved is g_tt p^t, not the flat-space p^t, and that a local observer measures the hatted component, not p^t.
Write hbar omega = -p.u_obs (22.12).
Static observer: spatial components zero, g_tt (u^t)^2 = -1 gives u^t = (1 - 2M/r)^{-1/2} (22.13, 22.14).
Key identity: u_obs(r) = (1 - 2M/r)^{-1/2} xi.
Hence hbar omega_R = (1 - 2M/R)^{-1/2}(-xi.p)_R (22.15), with the factor tending to 1 at infinity.
Conservation of xi.p along the geodesic equates the two brackets, giving (22.16).

sections.title: Motion in Schwarzschild spacetime
sections.summary: With a margin checklist of the tools alongside, Example 22.1 restricts to the equatorial plane and substitutes the constants of motion into the normalization condition. Rearranging gives an energy-like equation with effective energy (E-tilde^2 - 1)/2 and an effective potential -M/r + L^2/2r^2 - M L^2/r^3, identical in shape to the Newtonian problem of Chapter 20 apart from the last term. The potential has an inner maximum and plunges to minus infinity near the origin, which is where the new relativistic trajectories come from. Example 22.2 restores G and c and defines a Newtonian energy to show the extra term is a 1/c^2 correction. A margin note lists the static observer's vielbein, needed to turn coordinate components into measurements, and cautions that moving observers require a different frame.
concepts: Newtonian limit of the relativistic energy equation
key_moves: Checklist: u.u = -1 or 0; Killing rule gives conserved u_alpha; dx^i/dt = (1/u^0) dx^i/dtau (22.17).
Set theta = pi/2 and write u.u = -1 in components (22.18).
Replace u^t by E-tilde/(1 - 2M/r) and u^phi by L-tilde/r^2 (22.19).
Rearrange so the left side is the constant (E-tilde^2 - 1)/2 (22.20).
Expand the bracket into -M/r + L^2/2r^2 - M L^2/r^3 (22.21-22.23).
Compare with the Newtonian effective potential per unit mass (margin note) and with Fig. 22.3.
Restore G and c (22.24), introduce E_N (22.25), and obtain the Newtonian energy equation plus a 1/r^3 correction (22.26).
Quote static-observer vielbein components; they become unity at infinity so far-away measurements equal coordinate values.

sections.title: Example: the radial plunge
sections.summary: A massive particle released from rest at infinity falls straight in. Zero angular momentum and E-tilde = 1 give dt/dtau = (1 - 2M/r)^{-1} and, from the effective-potential equation, dr/dtau = -(2M/r)^{1/2}, so the four-velocity is fully determined. Margin notes construct the orthonormal frame carried by the falling particle and record the coordinate speed dr/dt, whose magnitude is the coordinate escape speed.
concepts: radial plunge from rest at infinity
conserved energy per unit rest mass
key_moves: Radial motion means L-tilde = 0; rest at infinity means u^t = 1 there, hence E-tilde = 1 and zero effective energy for the whole fall.
Effective-potential equation reduces to (1/2)(dr/dtau)^2 = M/r (22.28); choose the negative root for infall.
Margin: build the falling frame with e_t-hat = u and a radial unit vector orthogonal to it (22.30).

sections.title: Radial plunge: proper time versus coordinate time
sections.summary: Example 22.4 integrates the plunge twice. In proper time r falls as (tau_* - tau)^{2/3}, reaching r = 0 after a finite interval with nothing special at 2M. In Schwarzschild time, which is the time kept by a distant static observer, dt/dr picks up a factor (1 - 2M/r)^{-1}; integrating gives an expression with a logarithm that diverges at r = 2M. The distant bookkeeping therefore never sees the infaller cross 2M, a curiosity flagged for Chapter 25.
concepts: coordinate-time divergence at the Schwarzschild radius
key_moves: Separate variables in (22.28): r^{1/2} dr = -(2M)^{1/2} dtau, integrated up to r = 0 at tau_* (22.31).
Obtain r(tau) (22.32) and invert to tau(r) (22.33).
Chain rule dt/dr = u^t/u^r (22.35), with u^t blowing up at 2M.
Quote the integrated result (22.36); the book omits the steps (one route: substitute s = (r/2M)^{1/2} and use partial fractions).
Conclude: finite tau, infinite t to reach 2M; defer interpretation.

sections.title: Coordinate speed versus locally measured speed
sections.summary: Example 22.5 drops the assumption of starting from rest. Using u.u = -1 and the conserved u_t, the coordinate speed satisfies (dr/dt)^2 = (1 - 2M/r)^2 [1 - (1 - 2M/r)/u_t^2], which falls to zero as r approaches 2M. A static observer at radius r converts dt and dr with the vielbein factors, so the speed they measure is (1 - 2M/r)^{-1} dr/dt, and this tends to 1 (the speed of light) at 2M whatever the infall energy. The chapter concludes that normalization and two conservation laws already expose several strange relativistic effects.
concepts: locally measured speed of a static observer
transformation of 1-forms to an orthonormal frame
conserved energy per unit rest mass
key_moves: Factor (u^t)^2 out of u.u = -1 and convert dr/dtau into dr/dt (22.37).
Replace u^t by u_t using u_t = g_tt u^t and solve for (dr/dt)^2 (22.38).
Transform basis 1-forms: dt-hat = (1 - 2M/r)^{1/2} dt, dr-hat = (1 - 2M/r)^{-1/2} dr (22.39).
Divide to get the static observer's measured speed (22.40) and take r -> 2M.

sections.title: Chapter summary and exercises
sections.summary: The summary restates the three pillars: the normalized velocity with constants from the t and phi independence of the metric, the relativistic effective potential, and the four-velocity of a plunge from rest at infinity. Seven exercises follow, covering the acceleration of static particles, a full geodesic-equation cross-check, the redshift via vielbeins, the Newtonian limit, escape from a star's surface, the Hafele-Keating airborne clock effect, and the relative speed at which a dropped observer passes a static one.
concepts: proper acceleration of a static observer
relative velocity from the dot product of four-velocities
key_moves: Boxed plunge four-velocity (22.41).
Exercise 22.6 supplies approximate clock-rate formulas (22.42, 22.43) for ground and airborne clocks.

concepts.name: Schwarzschild metric
concepts.definition: The static, spherically symmetric vacuum solution of Einstein's equations outside a mass M; in Schwarzschild coordinates its only non-zero components are g_tt = -(1 - 2M/r), g_rr = (1 - 2M/r)^{-1}, g_theta theta = r^2 and g_phi phi = r^2 sin^2 theta (geometrized units).
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 21 at the very start and listed component by component in the margin so that the reader can inspect which coordinates appear.

concepts.name: geodesic equation
concepts.definition: Second-order equation d^2x^mu/dtau^2 + Gamma^mu_{alpha beta} (dx^alpha/dtau)(dx^beta/dtau) = 0 whose solutions are the world lines of freely falling particles; the connection coefficients come from derivatives of the metric.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled in a footnote as the apparently heavy route that the chapter intends to avoid; Exercise 22.2 asks the reader to confirm the shortcut against it.

concepts.name: four-velocity normalization
concepts.definition: For a massive particle whose world line is parametrized by proper time, the tangent four-velocity has fixed squared length g_{mu nu} u^mu u^nu = -1 (signature -+++); it acts as a first integral that fixes the particle type and replaces one component of the geodesic equation.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in the opening as a 'simple fact' and then used as the engine of every example: combined with the conserved quantities it yields the redshift normalization, the effective potential and the plunge velocities.

concepts.name: null tangent condition
concepts.definition: The tangent vector of a light ray's world line, parametrized by an affine parameter lambda, has zero squared length; equivalently ds^2 = 0 along the ray.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated alongside the massive-particle condition as the second option for 'what kind of particle is falling', and listed in the margin toolbox as a constraint for photon problems.

concepts.name: affine parameter
concepts.definition: A parameter along a geodesic in terms of which the geodesic equation takes its standard form; it is unique up to linear rescaling. Proper time serves for timelike geodesics; for null geodesics some other affine parameter lambda must be used because proper time does not advance.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned in passing when stating the two normalization conditions.

concepts.name: constants of the motion
concepts.definition: Quantities that keep the same value along a trajectory; for geodesics in a metric with symmetries they reduce the number of equations that must be integrated.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by the Newtonian orbit problem, where energy and angular momentum conservation make the problem solvable; the chapter promises the same simplification in relativity.

concepts.name: Killing vector field
concepts.definition: A vector field along which the metric does not change (its Lie derivative of the metric vanishes); it generates an isometry. In coordinates where no metric component depends on x^alpha, the basis vector e_alpha is a Killing vector.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced operationally through a boxed three-step recipe, explicitly without proof, with a margin pointer to the geometric treatment in Chapter 33.
concepts.notes: The recipe is sufficient but not necessary: a metric can have Killing vectors that are not coordinate basis vectors in the chosen chart. Proof deferred to GA ch33 §33.5.

concepts.name: conservation law from a Killing vector
concepts.definition: If xi is a Killing vector and u is the tangent of a geodesic, then xi.u is constant along the geodesic; in adapted coordinates this says the covariant component u_alpha is conserved whenever the metric does not depend on x^alpha.
concepts.how_introduced: Step 3 of the recipe, restated in the margin toolbox as the rule that independence from x^alpha conserves u_alpha; used for both massive particles (u) and photons (p).
concepts.notes: Not proved in this chapter; it is the relativistic analogue of a cyclic coordinate giving a conserved canonical momentum in Lagrangian mechanics.

concepts.name: time-translation Killing vector
concepts.definition: For a static metric, the vector xi = e_t with components (1, 0, 0, 0), reflecting the independence of the metric from t; at infinity it coincides with the four-velocity of a static observer.
concepts.how_introduced: Read off the Schwarzschild metric by step 2 of the recipe and later used to express any static observer's four-velocity as a rescaled xi.

concepts.name: rotational Killing vector
concepts.definition: The vector eta = e_phi with components (0, 0, 0, 1), expressing the independence of the Schwarzschild metric from the azimuthal angle phi.
concepts.how_introduced: Found by step 2 of the recipe alongside xi.

concepts.name: conserved energy per unit rest mass
aliases: energy at infinity per unit mass
concepts.definition: E-tilde = -xi.u = (1 - 2M/r) dt/dtau, constant along a Schwarzschild geodesic; for timelike geodesics it is the particle's total energy per unit rest mass as measured by a static observer at infinity (E-tilde = 1 for a particle at rest at infinity).
concepts.how_introduced: Defined as minus the conserved dot product with xi (sign chosen so it is positive), then interpreted via a margin argument that a static observer at infinity has four-velocity xi and measures energy -p.xi.
prerequisites: conservation law from a Killing vector
concepts.notes: Example 22.5 works with u_t, which equals minus E-tilde; only its square appears.

concepts.name: conserved angular momentum per unit rest mass
concepts.definition: L-tilde = eta.u = r^2 sin^2 theta dphi/dtau, constant along a Schwarzschild geodesic; in the equatorial plane it is r^2 dphi/dtau, formally the Newtonian angular momentum per unit mass with proper time replacing time.
concepts.how_introduced: Picked out as eta.u = u_phi and compared with the cylindrical-coordinate expression from mechanics.
prerequisites: conservation law from a Killing vector

concepts.name: energy measured by an observer
concepts.definition: A particle with four-momentum p has energy E = -p.u_obs in the rest frame of an observer with four-velocity u_obs; this is the time component of p in that observer's orthonormal frame.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated in a footnote on constants of motion to interpret E-tilde, then used as equation 22.12 for photon frequencies measured by static observers.

concepts.name: static observer
aliases: observer at rest with respect to the star
concepts.definition: An observer held at fixed r, theta, phi in the Schwarzschild geometry (necessarily accelerating unless at infinity); their four-velocity has only a time component u^t = (1 - 2M/r)^{-1/2}, so u_obs = (1 - 2M/r)^{-1/2} xi.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the two measuring stations of the redshift argument; normalization fixes the time component and yields the key identity with xi.
concepts.notes: Exercise 22.1 asks for the proper acceleration needed to stay static.

concepts.name: gravitational redshift
concepts.definition: Light sent from radius R to a distant static observer arrives with lower frequency, omega_inf = omega_R (1 - 2M/R)^{1/2}, because the conserved quantity is -xi.p while each static observer's measured energy carries a different normalization factor.
concepts.how_introduced: First application of the toolkit: two static observers and a radial photon (Fig. 22.1); presented as revisiting the equivalence-principle shift of Chapter 6 with the exact Schwarzschild factor.
prerequisites: conservation law from a Killing vector
concepts.notes: Exercise 22.3 reproduces it with vielbein components instead of the Killing-vector trick.

concepts.name: photon four-momentum
concepts.definition: The four-momentum p of light is a null vector tangent to the light ray's null geodesic, so the Killing conservation law applies to it just as to u for massive particles.
concepts.how_introduced: Assumed in a footnote (p parallel to u for light) so that xi.p is conserved; a careful treatment is promised for Section 24.7.

concepts.name: coordinate velocity
concepts.definition: The rate of change of spatial coordinates with coordinate time, obtained from the four-velocity as dx^i/dt = u^i/u^t; it is a bookkeeping quantity, not in general what any local observer measures.
concepts.how_introduced: Listed in the margin toolbox and used for the plunge (dt/dr and dr/dt) and for Example 22.5.

concepts.name: equatorial-plane reduction
concepts.definition: Because of spherical symmetry any geodesic can be rotated into the plane theta = pi/2, where u^theta = 0 and the problem involves only t, r and phi.
concepts.how_introduced: Adopted 'for simplicity' at the start of Example 22.1 without a detailed symmetry argument.

concepts.name: effective energy
concepts.definition: The constant (E-tilde^2 - 1)/2, playing the role of the total energy per unit mass in the one-dimensional radial equation; it is zero for a particle released from rest at infinity and positive for unbound particles.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined after rearranging the normalization condition so that the left-hand side is constant; the notation follows Hartle.
prerequisites: conserved energy per unit rest mass

concepts.name: relativistic effective potential
concepts.definition: The function V_eff(r) = -M/r + L^2/(2r^2) - M L^2/r^3 such that equatorial geodesics obey E_eff = (1/2)(dr/dtau)^2 + V_eff(r); compared with Newtonian gravity it contains an extra attractive term that dominates at small r, producing an inner maximum and a fall to minus infinity.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived in Example 22.1 from u.u = -1 plus the two conserved quantities, recognized as the same structure as Chapter 20's Newtonian problem, and plotted against the Newtonian curve in Fig. 22.3.
prerequisites: conserved energy per unit rest mass
conserved angular momentum per unit rest mass
concepts.notes: Radial variable is proper-time based: the equation is exact in tau, not in t.

concepts.name: relativistic 1/r^3 correction
concepts.definition: The term -M L^2/r^3 (GM L^2/(c^2 r^3) in ordinary units) that distinguishes the Schwarzschild effective potential from the Newtonian one; it is suppressed by 1/c^2 but overwhelms the centrifugal barrier at small r.
concepts.how_introduced: Singled out when comparing with the Newtonian effective potential and made explicit by restoring G and c in Example 22.2.

concepts.name: Newtonian effective potential
concepts.definition: For Newtonian motion under a point mass, V_eff = -M/r + L^2/(2r^2) per unit mass (with G = 1), combining gravitational and centrifugal terms so radial motion is one-dimensional.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled in a margin note from Chapter 20 with the factor of m explained, and drawn dotted in Fig. 22.3.

concepts.name: Newtonian limit of the relativistic energy equation
concepts.definition: Writing E-tilde = (mc^2 + E_N)/(mc^2) and restoring G and c turns the effective-potential equation into the Newtonian radial energy equation plus a correction of order 1/c^2 proportional to 1/r^3.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 22.2 carries out the substitution; Exercise 22.4 asks the reader to check it.
concepts.notes: The printed result silently drops a term E_N^2/(2mc^2) and identifies dtau with dt at leading order.

concepts.name: geometrized units
concepts.definition: Units in which G and c are set to one so that mass is measured as a length, M standing for GM/c^2; physical formulas are recovered by reinserting G and c by dimensional analysis.
concepts.how_introduced: Used throughout; Example 22.2 shows how to put the constants back into V_eff.

concepts.name: static-observer orthonormal frame (vielbein)
concepts.definition: The orthonormal basis carried by a static observer, related to Schwarzschild coordinate components by (e_t)^t-hat = (1 - 2M/r)^{1/2}, (e_r)^r-hat = (1 - 2M/r)^{-1/2}, (e_theta)^theta-hat = r, (e_phi)^phi-hat = r sin theta; hatted components are what that observer measures.
concepts.how_introduced: Listed in a margin note as the tool for converting coordinate results into measurements, with the remark that at infinity the time and radial factors are one; later used in Example 22.5.

concepts.name: transformation of 1-forms to an orthonormal frame
concepts.definition: Basis 1-forms transform with the vielbein as omega^mu-hat = (e_mu)^mu-hat omega^mu, so the static observer's time and radial displacement forms are rescaled coordinate forms.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled in Example 22.5 to get the local speed from the coordinate speed.

concepts.name: freely falling observer frame
concepts.definition: The orthonormal frame carried by a freely falling particle: its time vector is the particle's four-velocity and its radial vector is the unit vector in the t-r plane orthogonal to u; for the plunge from rest at infinity e_r-hat has coordinate components (-(2M/r)^{1/2}/(1 - 2M/r), 1, 0, 0).
concepts.how_introduced: Built in a margin note to Example 22.3, emphasizing that it is locally flat but moving relative to the static frame.
prerequisites: radial plunge from rest at infinity
concepts.notes: The angular vectors quoted with components (0,0,1,0) and (0,0,0,1) are not unit length; normalized versions carry 1/r and 1/(r sin theta).

concepts.name: radial plunge from rest at infinity
concepts.definition: The timelike geodesic with L-tilde = 0 and E-tilde = 1: u^mu = ((1 - 2M/r)^{-1}, -(2M/r)^{1/2}, 0, 0), so dr/dtau has the same form as the Newtonian infall speed from rest at infinity.
concepts.how_introduced: Chosen as the showcase example: all constants follow from the initial conditions, the equation of motion is a one-liner, and it exposes the proper-versus-coordinate time contrast.
prerequisites: conserved energy per unit rest mass

concepts.name: proper time of radial infall
concepts.definition: Along the plunge, tau(r) = tau_* - (2/3)(2M)^{-1/2} r^{3/2}, so reaching any smaller radius, including 2M and r = 0, takes a finite proper time; from r = 2M to r = 0 it is 4M/3.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained in Example 22.4 by separating variables in dr/dtau and plotted in Fig. 22.5.
prerequisites: radial plunge from rest at infinity

concepts.name: coordinate-time divergence at the Schwarzschild radius
aliases: frozen infall as seen from far away
concepts.definition: Schwarzschild time t, which matches the clocks of distant static observers, grows without bound as a radially falling particle approaches r = 2M, because dt/dtau = E-tilde/(1 - 2M/r) diverges; the particle's own clock records only a finite interval.
concepts.how_introduced: Read off the logarithm in the integrated t(r) (22.36) and Fig. 22.6, stated as the most notable curiosity, and deferred to Chapter 25.
concepts.notes: A statement about the Schwarzschild coordinate chart, not about any physical barrier; resolution in GA ch25 and ch27.

concepts.name: Schwarzschild radius
concepts.definition: The radius r = 2M (2GM/c^2) where g_tt vanishes and g_rr diverges in Schwarzschild coordinates; static observers cannot exist there.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears as the place where the redshift factor, the coordinate time and the local infall speed all misbehave; marked as a dotted line in Figs. 22.2, 22.6 and 22.7.

concepts.name: coordinate velocity of radial infall
concepts.definition: For radial geodesics with conserved u_t, (dr/dt)^2 = (1 - 2M/r)^2 [1 - (1 - 2M/r)/u_t^2]; it tends to zero as r -> 2M whatever the energy, and for release from rest at infinity it equals -(1 - 2M/r)(2M/r)^{1/2}.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived in Example 22.5 from the normalization condition written in terms of dr/dt, and plotted as the solid line in Fig. 22.7.
prerequisites: conserved energy per unit rest mass

concepts.name: locally measured speed of a static observer
concepts.definition: The radial speed of a passing particle measured by a static observer at the same r, dr-hat/dt-hat = (1 - 2M/r)^{-1} dr/dt; it tends to the speed of light as r -> 2M for any infall energy (for release from rest at infinity it equals (2M/r)^{1/2}).
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained in Example 22.5 by converting dt and dr with the static-observer vielbein, and drawn dashed in Fig. 22.7 next to the vanishing coordinate speed.

concepts.name: coordinate escape velocity
concepts.definition: The magnitude of dr/dt for a particle that just reaches infinity with zero speed, (1 - 2M/r)(2M/r)^{1/2}; by time reversal it equals the coordinate speed of the plunge from rest at infinity.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned in a footnote beside eqn 22.34 and pursued in Exercise 22.5, which asks for the escape speed and energy in the launcher's rest frame.

concepts.name: proper acceleration of a static observer
concepts.definition: The magnitude of the four-acceleration a = nabla_u u of an observer held at fixed r; it is non-zero because such an observer is not following a geodesic.
concepts.how_introduced: Only posed in Exercise 22.1, which asks for the acceleration components of a particle at rest and then its frame-measured value.

concepts.name: gravitational clock effect
concepts.definition: Clocks at different heights and speeds around the rotating Earth accumulate different proper times because of both the gravitational potential and their motion; eastward and westward flights differ because of the Earth's rotation.
concepts.how_introduced: Posed as Exercise 22.6 with approximate proper-time rate formulas; the authors note the Hafele-Keating flights of the early 1970s agreed with such predictions.

concepts.name: relative velocity from the dot product of four-velocities
concepts.definition: Two observers with four-velocities u and v passing at the same event have Lorentz factor of relative motion gamma = -u.v.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 2 in the hint to Exercise 22.7.

figures.label: Fig. 22.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: A light ray's world line crosses the world lines of a static observer at R and another at infinity.
figures.visual_description: Spacetime diagram with t vertical and r horizontal. Two straight vertical lines mark static world lines, one above the tick labelled R and one above the tick labelled infinity. A single smooth curve, rising gently from left to right and slightly concave downward, starts left of R and crosses both vertical lines, representing an outgoing radial photon.
figures.what_it_teaches: The redshift set-up: emission and reception are events on two different static world lines joined by one null geodesic, so the comparison is between two local measurements linked by a conserved quantity.

redesign.idea: Two-clock light ladder: a Schwarzschild t-r diagram with correctly curved outgoing null rays emitted periodically from a static emitter, and the tick marks of both static clocks spaced by proper time so the learner sees crests arrive further apart in the receiver's proper time.
redesign.interaction: Drag the emitter radius R toward 2M and the receiver radius outward; a readout shows the received-to-emitted frequency ratio sqrt(1 - 2M/R_emit)/sqrt(1 - 2M/R_rec); toggle between spacing the crests in coordinate time (identical at both ends) and in each observer's proper time (stretched at the receiver).

figures.label: Fig. 22.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: Frequency that must be measured at radius R to deliver a fixed frequency at infinity, for R outside 2M.
figures.visual_description: Graph with omega_R on the vertical axis and R on the horizontal axis, origin marked 0 on both axes. A dotted vertical line rises from R = 2M and a dotted horizontal line sits at height omega_infinity. A solid decreasing curve comes down from the top of the plot just right of the 2M line and flattens out, approaching the omega_infinity dotted level from above at large R.
figures.what_it_teaches: Redshift is negligible far out and becomes unbounded near r = 2M: light that arrives far away with a given frequency must have been extremely blueshifted locally when emitted close to 2M.

redesign.idea: Redshift ruler for real objects: plot the factor (1 - 2M/R)^{-1/2} against R/2M on a log axis with markers for Earth's surface, the Sun, a white dwarf and a neutron star, plus a draggable emitter.
redesign.interaction: Drag the emission radius; readouts show fractional shift z and the equivalent Doppler velocity; toggle between showing omega_R for fixed omega_inf and omega_inf for fixed omega_R; a colour swatch shifts from green toward red.

figures.label: Fig. 22.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: Schwarzschild effective potential for L-tilde/M = 4.3 (solid) against the Newtonian effective potential (dotted).
figures.visual_description: Axes labelled V_eff(r-vector) vertically and |r-vector| horizontally with a 0 level marked. Solid curve: starts far below the axis near the origin, climbs steeply to a tall narrow peak above zero, drops back below zero into a broad shallow well, then creeps up toward zero from below at large r. Dotted curve: descends from very large positive values at small r (starting just right of the solid peak), crosses zero, forms a well of similar location, and merges with the solid curve at large r.
figures.what_it_teaches: Relativity keeps the Newtonian well and outer behaviour but replaces the infinite centrifugal wall with a finite barrier followed by a plunge, so particles with enough energy or too little angular momentum can be captured.

redesign.idea: Effective-potential playground: live V_eff(r) with its three terms stacked in faint colours, the Newtonian curve for comparison, and a draggable energy line whose intersections mark turning points; a companion panel animates the corresponding orbit in the equatorial plane.
redesign.interaction: Slider for L-tilde/M (watch the barrier and well merge at L-tilde/M = sqrt(12) and vanish below it); drag the energy level E_eff; toggle each term on or off; click a point to launch a particle and see bound, scattered or captured motion.

figures.label: Fig. 22.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: Sketch of a particle falling straight in from infinity.
figures.visual_description: A thin vertical dotted line. At its top is the symbol for infinity with a solid dot just beneath and a short downward arrow; the letter r labels the middle of the line; the bottom ends at a short horizontal tick marked 0.
figures.what_it_teaches: Fixes the geometry of the example: purely radial motion from infinity to the centre, so angular momentum is zero.
concepts: radial plunge from rest at infinity

redesign.idea: Fold into the plunge dashboard: a radial track with the falling particle, a static observer stationed at an adjustable radius and a distant observer, each carrying a clock readout.
redesign.interaction: Play/scrub the fall; place the static observer anywhere outside 2M to see their local speed reading as the particle passes.

figures.label: Fig. 22.5
figures.caption_paraphrase: Proper time of the plunging particle plotted against its radial coordinate.
figures.visual_description: Axes with tau vertical and r horizontal, origin 0. A solid curve starts on the r axis at some initial radius (tau = 0) and rises to the left in a concave-down arc, reaching the tau axis at a finite height with a horizontal tangent. The tau axis itself is overdrawn with a zigzag line from the origin up to beyond where the curve meets it, indicating the singularity at r = 0. Nothing special is drawn at r = 2M. Note that the caption speaks of r evolving with tau, but the plot puts tau on the vertical axis and r on the horizontal one, mirroring the layout of Fig. 22.6.
figures.what_it_teaches: On the infaller's own clock the fall is smooth and finite all the way to r = 0; crossing 2M leaves no mark on proper time.
concepts: radial plunge from rest at infinity

redesign.idea: Twin-clock plunge plot: tau(r) and t(r) on shared r axis with a moving marker, so the learner sees one curve reach r = 0 while the other runs off to infinity at 2M.
redesign.interaction: Slider for starting radius (in units of M) and a scrubber along r; readouts give elapsed tau and t; a unit switch converts to seconds for a chosen black-hole mass.

figures.label: Fig. 22.6
figures.caption_paraphrase: Schwarzschild coordinate time for the same plunge against r, with the dotted line at r_S = 2M.
figures.visual_description: Axes with t vertical and r horizontal, origin 0, and a dotted vertical line at r_S close to the t axis. A solid curve starts on the r axis at the initial radius, climbs up and to the left almost straight, then bends sharply upward as it nears r_S and runs vertically alongside the dotted line off the top of the plot, never touching it.
figures.what_it_teaches: In Schwarzschild time the infaller approaches 2M asymptotically; the distant observer's bookkeeping never records the crossing.
concepts: coordinate-time divergence at the Schwarzschild radius

redesign.idea: Same twin-clock panel as Fig. 22.5, adding light signals: the infaller emits a pulse each proper second and the distant observer's reception times are plotted, spreading out without bound as r -> 2M.
redesign.interaction: Scrub proper time; watch received-pulse timestamps; toggle a log scale on t to reveal the logarithmic divergence.

figures.label: Fig. 22.7
figures.caption_paraphrase: For a radial plunge not starting from rest, coordinate speed dr/dt (solid) and the speed measured by a local static observer (dashed) against r.
figures.visual_description: Vertical axis labelled v-hat, v with ticks 0 and 1; horizontal axis r with a dotted vertical line at r_S. Dashed curve: starts at height 1 on the r_S line and decreases steadily, flattening toward about half the height of the 1 tick at large r. Solid curve: starts at 0 on the r_S line, rises almost vertically, levels off by a few r_S at just under the dashed curve (a very slight hump), and stays nearly flat, converging with the dashed curve at the right edge.
figures.what_it_teaches: The coordinate speed misleadingly vanishes at 2M while a local observer sees the particle approach the speed of light; far away both agree because the vielbein factors tend to one.
concepts: locally measured speed of a static observer

redesign.idea: Speed-versus-radius explorer with an energy slider: dr/dt and dr-hat/dt-hat for bound (drop from finite r), marginal (E-tilde = 1) and unbound infall, with a marker at the maximum of the coordinate speed (r = 6M for E-tilde = 1).
redesign.interaction: Slider for E-tilde (or release radius); hover to read both speeds; toggle a third curve for the speed measured by the infaller relative to static observers to show it equals the dashed line.

worked_examples.label: Killing vectors and constants of motion for Schwarzschild (§22.1, in prose)
worked_examples.problem: Identify the symmetries of the Schwarzschild metric and the quantities conserved along its geodesics.
worked_examples.method: Apply the three-step rule: none of the components involve t or phi, so e_t and e_phi are Killing vectors; dot each into u using g_{mu nu} = e_mu.e_nu and the diagonal metric.
worked_examples.key_insight: Conserved quantities are simply the lowered components u_t and u_phi; no Christoffel symbols are needed.
worked_examples.result: E-tilde = (1 - 2M/r) dt/dtau and L-tilde = r^2 sin^2 theta dphi/dtau are constant along geodesics.
concepts: conservation law from a Killing vector
conserved energy per unit rest mass
conserved angular momentum per unit rest mass

worked_examples.label: Gravitational redshift derivation (§22.2, in prose)
worked_examples.problem: Relate the frequency of a radially outgoing photon measured by a static observer at R to that measured by a static observer at infinity.
worked_examples.method: Use hbar omega = -p.u_obs; normalize the static observer's velocity to get u_obs = (1 - 2M/r)^{-1/2} xi; use conservation of xi.p along the null geodesic to equate the two evaluations.
worked_examples.key_insight: The static observer's four-velocity is parallel to the time Killing vector, so each measured frequency is a conserved number times a local normalization factor.

worked_examples.label: Example 22.1
worked_examples.problem: Reduce equatorial motion of a massive particle in Schwarzschild spacetime to a one-dimensional radial equation.
worked_examples.method: Set theta = pi/2, write u.u = -1 in components, replace u^t and u^phi by E-tilde and L-tilde, and rearrange so that a constant equals a kinetic-like term plus a function of r.
worked_examples.key_insight: The normalization condition is itself the first integral of the radial geodesic equation once the two conserved quantities are inserted.
worked_examples.result: (E-tilde^2 - 1)/2 = (1/2)(dr/dtau)^2 + V_eff(r) with V_eff = -M/r + L^2/(2r^2) - M L^2/r^3.

worked_examples.label: Example 22.2
worked_examples.problem: Show how the relativistic radial energy equation relates to the Newtonian one.
worked_examples.method: Reinsert G and c in V_eff, define a Newtonian energy by E-tilde = (mc^2 + E_N)/mc^2, multiply through by mc^2 and write L = m L-tilde.
worked_examples.key_insight: Every Newtonian term reappears, and relativity contributes one additional attractive term suppressed by 1/c^2 and growing as 1/r^3.
worked_examples.result: E_N = (m/2)(dr/dtau)^2 + L^2/(2mr^2) - GMm/r - GML^2/(mc^2 r^3), valid to leading order in E_N/mc^2.
concepts: Newtonian limit of the relativistic energy equation

worked_examples.label: Example 22.3
worked_examples.problem: Find the four-velocity of a massive particle that falls radially from rest at infinity.
worked_examples.method: Radial motion gives L-tilde = 0; rest at infinity gives u^t = 1 there, so E-tilde = 1 and zero effective energy for the whole fall; E-tilde fixes u^t and the effective-potential equation fixes u^r with the inward sign.
worked_examples.key_insight: Initial conditions at infinity pin both constants, so the entire four-velocity follows algebraically without integrating anything.
concepts: radial plunge from rest at infinity
conserved energy per unit rest mass

worked_examples.label: Example 22.4
worked_examples.problem: Compute how much proper time and how much Schwarzschild coordinate time elapse during the radial plunge.
worked_examples.method: Separate variables in dr/dtau = -(2M/r)^{1/2} and integrate to the arrival time tau_* at r = 0; for t, form dt/dr = u^t/u^r and integrate. The book states the logarithmic result without steps; a tutor can supply them with s = (r/2M)^{1/2} and partial fractions.
worked_examples.key_insight: The factor (1 - 2M/r)^{-1} in u^t makes the coordinate-time integral diverge logarithmically at 2M, while the proper-time integrand is perfectly regular there.
worked_examples.result: r(tau) = (3/2)^{2/3}(2M)^{1/3}(tau_* - tau)^{2/3}; t(r) given by (22.36), which tends to infinity as r -> 2M.
concepts: coordinate-time divergence at the Schwarzschild radius

worked_examples.label: Example 22.5
worked_examples.problem: For radial infall with arbitrary energy, find the coordinate speed dr/dt and the speed measured by a static observer at the same radius.
worked_examples.method: Pull (u^t)^2 out of the normalization condition to convert dr/dtau into dr/dt, express u^t via the conserved u_t, solve for (dr/dt)^2; then rescale dt and dr with the static-observer vielbein 1-forms and divide.
worked_examples.key_insight: Coordinate speed is a chart artefact that vanishes at 2M; the physically measured speed is larger by (1 - 2M/r)^{-1} and approaches c there for every initial speed.
concepts: locally measured speed of a static observer
transformation of 1-forms to an orthonormal frame

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Newtonian orbit problems become easy once energy and angular momentum conservation are used
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Sets expectations that the relativistic problem, which looks like a system of coupled geodesic equations, can be cut down in the same way, and that close cousins of energy and angular momentum will be conserved.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Relativistic 'energy' E-tilde includes rest energy and is defined relative to a static observer at infinity; conservation follows from metric symmetry, not from a force law.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Split-screen: a Newtonian orbit and a Schwarzschild orbit with identical initial data, each with a live bar showing its conserved quantities staying fixed while r and phi change.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: L-tilde = r^2 dphi/dtau mirrors angular momentum per unit mass in cylindrical coordinates
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: conserved angular momentum per unit rest mass
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Reassures the reader that the Killing-vector construction reproduces a familiar expression in the equatorial plane.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The derivative is with respect to proper time and r is the areal radius, not a Euclidean distance.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A photon loses energy as it climbs out of the gravitational potential
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Offered in one sentence after the derivation as a heuristic for why the frequency drops; the book gives no mechanical picture beyond 'climbing the potential' (a thrown-ball comparison is a natural tutor extension, not the book's).
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The photon's speed does not change and nothing is 'lost' locally; the effect is really a comparison of clocks at different radii linked by the conserved xi.p.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Toggle between a 'climbing ball' cartoon and the two-clock picture, prompting learners to say which quantity is actually conserved.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The relativistic radial equation is a particle rolling in a one-dimensional potential, exactly as in Chapter 20
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The derived equation is cast in the familiar 'energy = kinetic + effective potential' shape so the reader can reuse turning-point and well reasoning, and the new behaviour is read off the shape of V_eff.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The 'time' is proper time, the 'energy' is (E-tilde^2 - 1)/2 rather than a physical energy, and the equation gives r(tau) but says nothing directly about phi(t) or what distant observers see.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Bead-on-a-wire animation: a bead slides on a wire shaped like V_eff while the orbit is traced in a side panel; reshape the wire with the L-tilde slider.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Plunge from rest at infinity has dr/dtau = -(2M/r)^{1/2}, the same form as Newtonian free fall from infinity (escape speed)
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: radial plunge from rest at infinity
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Implicit in eqn 22.28, which is the Newtonian energy statement for zero total energy; lets learners recognize the result before seeing the relativistic twists.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The match is with proper time and Schwarzschild r; in coordinate time the motion is very different near 2M.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Overlay Newtonian r(t) and relativistic r(tau) and r(t) for the same release; the first two coincide exactly, the third peels away near 2M.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: To find orbits in general relativity you must first compute all connection coefficients and solve the four coupled geodesic equations.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Two conserved quantities from the metric's symmetries plus the normalization of the four-velocity supply three first integrals, enough for equatorial motion; the geodesic equation is only a cross-check.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Earlier chapters present the geodesic equation as the law of free fall, and it is the general route.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The conserved photon energy along a geodesic is the coordinate component p^t, as in flat space.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: What stays constant is g_tt p^t = -xi.p; p^t itself changes with r.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In special relativity p^t is the energy and is conserved for free particles.
concepts: conservation law from a Killing vector

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: An observer at radius r measures the coordinate component p^t of a photon's momentum as its energy.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Measurement gives the component in the observer's orthonormal frame, -p.u_obs, which differs from p^t by the factor (1 - 2M/r)^{1/2} for a static observer.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Coordinate components look like the physical ones, and far from the mass they coincide.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Because a distant observer's time coordinate runs to infinity, an infalling astronaut never actually reaches r = 2M.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The astronaut's proper time to reach 2M and even r = 0 is finite; the divergence belongs to the Schwarzschild time coordinate, whose meaning is examined in Chapter 25.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Schwarzschild t matches the clocks of observers far away, so it feels like 'real' time.
concepts: coordinate-time divergence at the Schwarzschild radius

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: An infalling particle slows down and stops as it approaches r = 2M.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Only dr/dt vanishes; a static observer at the same radius measures the particle rushing past at a speed approaching c.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: dr/dt looks like an ordinary velocity and its graph drops to zero.
concepts: locally measured speed of a static observer

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The static-observer vielbein can be used to convert components for any observer at that radius.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Each observer's measurements require their own orthonormal frame; a moving (for example freely falling) observer needs a different vielbein.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: At a given r the metric is the same, so one may think the frame is too.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: E-tilde is the particle's energy as measured by whoever is nearby.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: E-tilde is energy per unit rest mass relative to a static observer at infinity; a local static observer measures E-tilde divided by (1 - 2M/r)^{1/2}.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: It is called 'energy' and is conserved, like the everyday notion.
concepts: conserved energy per unit rest mass

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The relativistic effective potential is just the Newtonian one with a small correction everywhere, so orbits change only slightly.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: At large r the correction is tiny, but at small r the -ML^2/r^3 term beats the centrifugal term, so the potential has a finite maximum and then falls without limit: a particle with energy above the barrier is captured whatever its angular momentum, whereas in Newtonian gravity any nonzero angular momentum prevents reaching r = 0.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Example 22.2 stresses that the extra term is order 1/c^2.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A metric has a symmetry only if some coordinate is missing from its components.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The recipe finds symmetries adapted to the chosen coordinates; Schwarzschild has two further rotational Killing vectors not visible as missing coordinates, and a clumsy chart can hide even t-independence.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The chapter's recipe is simple and presented as the way to find conserved quantities.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The r in V_eff is the distance from the centre, as the axis label |r| in Fig. 22.3 suggests.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: r is the Schwarzschild areal coordinate (circumference over 2 pi); radial proper distance differs from differences in r near the mass.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Newtonian intuition and the vector notation on the plot.

thought_experiments.name: Two static observers comparing a light signal
thought_experiments.setup: A static observer at radius R emits radial light of known locally measured frequency; a static observer far away measures the frequency received.
thought_experiments.lesson: Measured frequencies differ by the ratio of the observers' normalization factors because the only thing carried unchanged along the ray is -xi.p.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Slide the emitter toward 2M and watch the received wave stretch while both local clocks tick normally in their own frames.

thought_experiments.name: Astronaut dropped from rest at infinity
thought_experiments.setup: A particle starts at rest very far away and falls radially toward a compact mass; its own clock and the Schwarzschild time of distant observers are compared, and static observers along the way measure its speed.
thought_experiments.lesson: Proper time to reach 2M and r = 0 is finite, coordinate time diverges at 2M, and local observers see the speed approach c while dr/dt goes to zero.
concepts: radial plunge from rest at infinity
coordinate-time divergence at the Schwarzschild radius
locally measured speed of a static observer
thought_experiments.app_idea: Three synchronized panels (infaller's clock, distant clock, local speedometer) driven by one scrubber.

thought_experiments.name: Clocks flown east and west around the equator
thought_experiments.setup: Exercise 22.6: compare a clock on the ground at the equator with one flown at altitude around the Earth eastward and then westward.
thought_experiments.lesson: Height makes the airborne clock run faster, speed relative to the non-rotating frame makes it run slower; Earth's rotation makes eastward and westward results differ in sign and size.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Globe with two planes and three clocks; sliders for altitude and speed show accumulated nanoseconds for each direction.

thought_experiments.name: A dropped observer passing a static one
thought_experiments.setup: Exercise 22.7: two observers on the same radial line are at rest at r_1 and r_2 > r_1; the outer one is released and falls past the inner one.
thought_experiments.lesson: Relative speed at the meeting event follows from the dot product of their four-velocities, combining the conserved energy of the faller with the static observer's normalization.
concepts: relative velocity from the dot product of four-velocities
conserved energy per unit rest mass
thought_experiments.app_idea: Drag r_1 and r_2; show both four-velocity arrows in the t-r plane at the meeting point and the resulting gamma.

historical_notes.event: Flew caesium-beam clocks around the world once eastward and once westward on scheduled airliners (1971) and compared them with ground clocks; the book mentions only that the early-1970s experiment matched the exercise's predictions, the flight details are added context.
historical_notes.significance: Confirmed the combined gravitational and kinematic clock-rate effects that Exercise 22.6 asks the reader to estimate.

applications_and_observations.topic: Size of gravitational redshift for real objects
applications_and_observations.details: Our own estimates from eqn 22.16 (not in the book): fractional shift is roughly M/R when M/R is small.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Earth surface GM/(c^2 R) ~ 7e-10; Sun ~ 2.1e-6; white dwarf such as Sirius B ~ 3e-4 (about 80 km/s equivalent); 1.4 solar-mass neutron star with R = 10 km: 2M/R ~ 0.41, redshift z ~ 0.3.

applications_and_observations.details: Exercise 22.6 derives approximate proper-time rate differences for an aircraft at height h and speed v versus a clock on the rotating Earth, and notes the early-1970s flights agreed with such predictions.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Our estimate with h = 10 km, v = 230 m/s, equatorial rotation speed 465 m/s: rate difference about +0.4e-12 eastward (flying clock loses) and about -2e-12 westward (flying clock gains), i.e. tens to hundreds of nanoseconds over a roughly 45-hour circumnavigation; the published measurements were about -59 ns east and +273 ns west.

applications_and_observations.topic: Infall time from the horizon to r = 0
applications_and_observations.details: Our own evaluation of eqn 22.33 for release from rest at infinity: the proper time from r = 2M to r = 0 is 4M/3, i.e. (4/3) GM/c^3.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: About 6.6 microseconds per solar mass: ~66 microseconds for a 10 solar-mass black hole, ~28 s for Sagittarius A* (4.3 million solar masses), ~12 hours for M87* (6.5 billion solar masses).

applications_and_observations.topic: Features of the effective potential in Fig. 22.3
applications_and_observations.details: Our computation for L-tilde/M = 4.3: extrema of V_eff occur where r^2 - L^2 r + 3L^2 M^2 = 0 (units of M).
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Barrier maximum near r = 3.8M with V_eff about +0.04; well minimum near r = 14.7M with V_eff about -0.031; Newtonian minimum at r = L^2/M = 18.5M with V = -0.027. The printed barrier looks much taller relative to the well than these numbers, so the sketch is qualitative. Barrier and well merge when L-tilde/M = sqrt(12).

applications_and_observations.details: Our own evaluation of eqn 22.34: for release from rest at infinity |dr/dt| = (1 - 2M/r)(2M/r)^{1/2} peaks and then falls to zero at 2M, while the locally measured speed (2M/r)^{1/2} rises monotonically to 1.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Peak coordinate speed 2/(3 sqrt 3) ~ 0.385 c at r = 6M; locally measured speed at r = 6M is ~0.577 c.

applications_and_observations.topic: Smallness of the relativistic correction in the Solar System
applications_and_observations.details: Our estimate: the ratio of the 1/r^3 term to the centrifugal term in eqn 22.26 is 2GM/(c^2 r).
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: About 5e-8 at Mercury's orbit, which is why its effect shows up only as a slow cumulative perihelion precession (Chapter 23).

notation_and_conventions.convention: Geometrized units G = c = 1 throughout; M means GM/c^2 and has dimensions of length. Example 22.2 shows how to restore G and c.
Signature (-,+,+,+); coordinates ordered (t, r, theta, phi) with u^0 = u^t.
E-tilde and L-tilde denote energy and angular momentum per unit rest mass; E-tilde = -xi.u carries a minus sign so it is positive. Physical angular momentum L = m L-tilde.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Follows Hartle's notation; the authors warn other books define these terms differently.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Script E = (E-tilde^2 - 1)/2 is the constant in the radial equation, distinct from E-tilde and from the Newtonian E_N.
xi for the time-translation Killing vector e_t and eta for the rotational one e_phi.
tau (proper time) for massive particles; lambda for an affine parameter on null geodesics; overdot denotes d/dtau (as in L-tilde = r^2 phi-dot).
Hats label components in an observer's orthonormal frame; vielbein components are written (e_mu)^mu-hat and basis 1-forms transform as omega^mu-hat = (e_mu)^mu-hat omega^mu.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Bold d denotes a basis 1-form (dt, dr), plain d an ordinary differential.

notation_and_conventions.convention: r_S = 2M, drawn as a dotted line on the plunge graphs.
Some numbered equations sit in the margin rather than the main text: 22.1 (metric components), 22.17 (coordinate-velocity trick), 22.30 and 22.34 (plunge footnotes); 22.1 is printed beside 22.2.
notation_and_conventions.notes: The reading copy lists 22.2 before 22.1 for this reason.

notation_and_conventions.convention: hbar omega = -p.u_obs, with p the null four-momentum and omega angular frequency.

margin_notes.summary: Epigraphs from John Webster's The Duchess of Malfi (humans as tennis balls of the stars) and Chaucer's Canterbury Tales prologue (the urge to go on pilgrimage), setting a light tone for a chapter on journeys through curved spacetime.
The Schwarzschild metric components are listed separately so they can be scanned for coordinate dependence.
Reminder of the geodesic equation, whose connection coefficients come from the metric.
Reminder: proper time labels points on a massive particle's world line, so the four-velocity components are the tau-derivatives of t, r, theta and phi.
Pointer: Killing vectors receive a proper geometric treatment in Chapter 33.
Reminder that metric components are dot products of coordinate basis vectors.

Energy measured by an observer is -p.u; a static observer at infinity has four-velocity equal to xi because space is flat there, so the energy they measure is -p.xi, which justifies reading E-tilde as energy at infinity.
Gravitational redshift is the second of three frequency-shift mechanisms first met in Chapter 6, alongside Doppler and cosmological shifts.

Conservation of p.xi for light relies on assuming p is parallel to the tangent u; the footnote points to 'Section 24.7' for more on photon momentum, which in the chapter as printed is Example 24.7 inside §24.2.

An alternative route to the redshift uses vielbein components to convert p^t into the locally measured energy (left as an exercise); the main text instead folds the Killing vector into the observer's velocity because two distant measurements are being linked.
Footnote 8 recalls that the time Killing vector has components (1,0,0,0), which is what lets the static observer's velocity be written as a rescaled xi.

Margin checklist beside the opening of §22.3 (not boxed): u.u = -1 for massive particles, u.u = 0 and ds = 0 for photons, the Killing rule for conserved u_alpha, and dx^i/dt = (1/u^0) dx^i/dtau (eqn 22.17 is numbered in the margin).
Caution that many books use this approach with different conventions; the chapter follows Hartle's approach and notation.
Particles arriving from infinity have E-tilde above 1 and hence positive effective energy.
The Newtonian effective potential energy of Chapter 20 differs by a factor of m from the per-unit-mass potential used here; relativity adds a 1/r^3 term.
Static-observer vielbein components listed, with a caution that a moving observer such as a free faller needs a different vielbein.
At rest at infinity means u^mu = (1,0,0,0) there, so E-tilde = 1 and the effective energy is zero throughout the plunge.
Radial infall has no way to acquire angular velocity, so the angular velocity components are zero.
Construction of the infaller's own orthonormal frame: time vector equal to u, angular vectors chosen along the coordinate directions, radial vector (22.30) orthogonal to u.
The integration constant in the proper-time solution is fixed by specifying r at one proper time.
The coordinate speed of the plunge (22.34) is recorded; its magnitude is the coordinate escape velocity explored in the exercises.

difficulty.notes: Algebra is light: substitutions into u.u = -1, one separable ODE and one partial-fraction integral. Conceptual demands come from the recipe being unproved, from keeping track of which quantities are coordinate components and which are measured, and from the vielbein and 1-form steps in Example 22.5, which are terse. The margin footnotes carry essential arguments (energy at infinity, the falling frame) that a hurried reader may skip. Minor printed slips: footnote 10 says E-tilde > 1 where E-tilde >= 1 is meant, footnote 14's angular basis vectors are not normalized, and eqn 22.26 is only a leading-order equality.
