teaching_gems.gem: A three-step, inspection-only recipe for conserved quantities: find coordinates missing from the metric, promote each to a Killing vector, dot it into the velocity.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Converts an abstract symmetry concept into an action a beginner can perform in seconds, and transfers to any metric they meet later (FRW, Kerr).
teaching_gems.app_idea: Metric inspector: learner pastes or selects a metric; each component is shown as a card, coordinates appearing in any card light up, the absent ones are offered as Killing vectors, and the corresponding conserved u_alpha expression is generated.

teaching_gems.gem: Writing a static observer's four-velocity as (1 - 2M/r)^{-1/2} times the time Killing vector, so the redshift becomes a ratio of normalization factors.
teaching_gems.why_effective: The whole derivation shrinks to one line and makes clear that the effect is a comparison of two local clocks linked by one conserved number.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Arrow diagram in the t-r plane showing xi as the same arrow everywhere and the static observer's unit u_obs as xi stretched by a radius-dependent factor that grows toward 2M.

teaching_gems.gem: Substituting E-tilde and L-tilde into u.u = -1 turns geodesic motion into the Chapter 20 effective-potential problem with a single extra term.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Reuses a mental model the learner already owns and localizes all the new physics in one visible term.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Term-by-term potential builder: sliders fade each of the three V_eff terms in and out so the learner watches the Newtonian curve morph into the relativistic one.

teaching_gems.gem: Restoring G and c and defining E_N through E-tilde = (mc^2 + E_N)/mc^2 to exhibit the relativistic term as an order-1/c^2 correction.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Shows exactly how general relativity contains Newtonian orbits as a limit, and gives a quantitative sense of when relativity matters.
teaching_gems.app_idea: A 'speed of light' slider that increases c from its true value toward infinity, collapsing the relativistic curve onto the Newtonian one, with a readout of 2GM/(c^2 r) at a chosen radius.

teaching_gems.gem: The radial plunge told through three graphs of one trajectory: r against proper time (finite), r against Schwarzschild time (diverges at 2M), and speed against r (coordinate speed to zero, local speed to c).
teaching_gems.why_effective: The contrast between chart quantities and measured quantities becomes visual and unforgettable, preparing the ground for the horizon chapter.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Plunge dashboard with one scrubber controlling all three plots plus an animated radial track; mass slider converts to seconds and km.

teaching_gems.gem: Initial conditions at infinity fix all constants (L-tilde = 0, E-tilde = 1), so the plunge four-velocity follows algebraically with no integration.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Demonstrates the power of conserved quantities: a relativistic trajectory problem reduces to reading off components.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Step-through derivation card where each click applies one fact (radial, at rest at infinity, normalization) and fills in one slot of u^mu.

teaching_gems.gem: Consistently distinguishing coordinate components from what an observer measures, using vielbein factors that become one at infinity.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Addresses the single most common confusion in Schwarzschild physics and gives a concrete conversion rule.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Toggle on every plot between 'coordinate' and 'measured by static observer here', with the conversion factor displayed and animated as r changes.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The Killing-vector conservation rule is used without any justification, and the recipe is only a sufficient condition in the chosen coordinates.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may treat it as magic, misapply it to non-geodesic motion, or conclude a metric has no symmetry when a coordinate change would reveal one.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Give a two-line reason: lower the geodesic equation, note du_alpha/dtau = (1/2) partial_alpha g_{mu nu} u^mu u^nu, which vanishes when g is independent of x^alpha. Point to Chapter 33 for the covariant version.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Footnote 10 says particles coming in from infinity have E-tilde > 1, yet Section 22.4 treats a particle from rest at infinity with E-tilde = 1 and zero effective energy.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Apparent contradiction about the marginally bound case.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: State E-tilde >= 1 for particles that reach infinity, with equality for release from rest there; E-tilde < 1 means bound.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Eqn 22.26 is written as an equality, but multiplying (E-tilde^2 - 1)/2 by mc^2 gives E_N + E_N^2/(2mc^2); the quadratic term is dropped, and proper time is kept where a Newtonian reader expects coordinate time.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Readers attempting Exercise 22.4 may fail to reproduce the exact equation.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Label it a leading-order result in E_N/mc^2 and note dtau ~ dt at that order.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Fig. 22.3 labels its axes with a vector r and |r|, and the barrier appears much taller than the well; for L-tilde/M = 4.3 the actual barrier height is only about +0.04 versus a well depth of about -0.03.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Encourages Euclidean reading of the Schwarzschild r and misjudges which energies are captured.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Plot to scale in units of M, label the axis r (areal coordinate), and mark the energy of a particle at rest at infinity (E_eff = 0).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Footnote 14 chooses the falling frame's angular basis vectors with components (0,0,1,0) and (0,0,0,1), which are not unit vectors; orthonormality requires 1/r and 1/(r sin theta). The reading-copy OCR additionally labels both as phi-hat.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners who check orthonormality get inconsistent results and doubt the method.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use (e_theta-hat)^mu = (0,0,1/r,0) and (e_phi-hat)^mu = (0,0,0,1/(r sin theta)); the radial vector (22.30) is correctly normalized.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The constant t_* in eqn 22.36 is described as the coordinate time at r = 0, but the formula has separate branches outside and inside 2M separated by a logarithmic divergence, so one constant cannot physically link them.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Suggests Schwarzschild time is a continuous, meaningful clock through the horizon.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Treat the exterior branch alone, with t_* an arbitrary offset, and state that Schwarzschild t is not a good coordinate across 2M (Chapters 25 and 27).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The step 'dr/dt equals the ratio of bold 1-forms dr/dt' in Example 22.5 is notationally loose; 1-forms cannot be divided.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Confusion about what operation turns the vielbein 1-form relations into a speed.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Say: apply both 1-forms to the particle's tangent vector (or displacement); the ratio of the resulting numbers gives dr-hat/dt-hat.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Fig. 22.7 calls the dashed curve a 'coordinate velocity' although it is the physically measured speed, and neither caption nor text states the energy used; the solid curve tends to about half the speed of light far away, so the example is an unbound plunge (E-tilde of roughly 1.1 by our reading).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Blurs the very distinction the example is meant to teach, and learners may try to match it to the E-tilde = 1 plunge.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Relabel as local speed measured by static observers and state the energy; also show the E-tilde = 1 case, where local speed is sqrt(2M/r) and coordinate speed peaks at r = 6M.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Example 22.5 switches from E-tilde to u_t without reminding the reader that u_t = -E-tilde.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Momentary confusion about a new constant; sign worries.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Write (u_t)^2 = E-tilde^2 explicitly and present the neat form (dr-hat/dt-hat)^2 = 1 - (1 - 2M/r)/E-tilde^2.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The plunge integrals run to r = 0 while the static-observer interpretation (and the Schwarzschild coordinates' timelike t) fails inside 2M; the chapter postpones all discussion.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may apply static-observer ideas or the redshift formula inside the horizon.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add an explicit flag: formulas involving static observers or 1 - 2M/r under a square root are valid only for r > 2M.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The photon's momentum is simply assumed tangent to the null geodesic, and the affine parameter normalization for light is not discussed.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Unclear why xi.p rather than some rescaled quantity is conserved.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Note that choosing lambda so that p = dx/dlambda makes p the tangent, and any affine rescaling only multiplies the conserved number by a constant.

tutor_notes: Open with: 'In Newtonian gravity, what two numbers make planetary orbits easy to solve, and why are they conserved?' Then ask what in the Schwarzschild metric could play the role of time-translation and rotation symmetry.

Order of explanation: (1) scan the metric for missing coordinates, (2) define E-tilde and L-tilde, (3) normalization u.u = -1 or 0, (4) redshift as a quick win, (5) effective potential, (6) radial plunge and its three clocks. Resist starting from the geodesic equation.
Before the redshift, check the learner can compute a measured energy as -p.u_obs in special relativity; if not, review that first, since the whole argument hinges on it.
Check for understanding after 22.1: 'Which component of u is conserved if the metric did not depend on theta?' and 'Why is E-tilde defined with a minus sign?'

When presenting V_eff, have the learner predict what happens to a particle with small angular momentum before showing the plot; then contrast the Newtonian infinite centrifugal wall with the finite relativistic barrier.
Keep a running two-column table 'coordinate quantity' versus 'measured by someone', filling in dt/dtau, p^t, dr/dt against proper time, hbar omega, dr-hat/dt-hat.

Common learner question: 'Does the astronaut ever cross the horizon?' Answer: yes, in finite proper time; the infinite t is a feature of the distant observer's coordinate labels. Promise the full story (tortoise and Kruskal coordinates) rather than overloading now.

Common learner question: 'If dr/dt goes to zero, does the particle hover at 2M?' Walk through 22.40: the local static observer sees it pass at nearly c, and static observers themselves become impossible at 2M.

Use concrete numbers to anchor scales: solar redshift about 2 parts per million, neutron-star surface z about 0.3, horizon-to-centre fall of about 6.6 microseconds per solar mass (tutor-computed estimates, not from the book).

For advanced learners, show the two-line proof that u_alpha is conserved when the metric is independent of x^alpha, and mention that Schwarzschild has two more rotational Killing vectors not visible as missing coordinates.
For novices, skip the falling-frame vielbein (22.30) and the 1-form language in Example 22.5; state the conversion factors for static observers as 'clock rate factor' and 'ruler factor' instead.
Point out the minor errata when they come up: E-tilde >= 1 (not > 1) for particles from infinity, eqn 22.26 holds to leading order, and footnote 14's angular basis vectors need 1/r factors.
